- **[P0] (obsolete) secded_ecc is Hamming(72,64) not SECDED: double-bit errors are silently 'healed' with wrong data** — `include/quickcpplib/algorithm/secded_ecc.hpp:164`
  - why not fixed: CONFIRMED by repro (see below), but the repair changes the ECC wire format. `secded_ecc<4096>` is a Hamming code because it has Hamming parity bits only - there is no overall-parity bit - so `verify()` can compute no syndrome that distinguishes a 1-bit from a 2-bit error, and a 3-bit alias is a valid codeword. Measured on the unmodified tree: of 489 two-bit flips, 471 returned `healed` with the buffer NOT equal to the original (silently healed to a different valid codeword) and only 18 returned `corrupt`. A real SECDED needs one extra overall-parity bit, which changes `result_bits_valid()` and every stored ECC for existing users (LLFIO-style filing system code), so it needs a maintainer decision: add the bit (format break), or add a new class/template parameter and deprecate this one. Repro kept at /workspace/ecc-test/db.cpp.
  - obsolete: closed by the rename, not by a code change. The class is now `hamming_ecc` in `include/quickcpplib/algorithm/hamming_ecc.hpp`, and its class documentation now states plainly that it is a single-error-correcting Hamming code with no overall-parity bit: it cannot detect a double-bit error (the syndrome aliases to a third position, `verify()` flips it, the block becomes a different valid codeword and `healed` is returned), three-bit errors can also land on a valid codeword, so it must be paired with a strong hash and must never be the thing which says a block is intact. The user decided NOT to implement real SECDED - the class has no production users - so the wire-format objection below no longer binds: an honest name and honest docs are the whole fix. Behaviour is UNCHANGED: two-bit errors still corrupt silently, that is simply documented now instead of being contradicted by the name.

- **[P1] (obsolete) QUICKCPPLIB_USE_SYSTEM_BYTE_LITE=ON is silently discarded on C++17 builds while the cache keeps showing ON** — `CMakeLists.txt:29`
  - also: `CMakeLists.txt:30` (was P2/open) QUICKCPPLIB_USE_SYSTEM_SPAN_LITE/BYTE_LITE silently forced OFF in the documented vcpkg/C++20 case

  - reverted: deleting the option and the bundled byte-lite tree (`headers: delete the bundled byte-lite polyfill`) was itself REVERTED (the `Revert "headers: delete the bundled byte-lite polyfill"` commit) - Outcome still has to build at C++14 and quickcpplib is shared between it and LLFIO, so the C++17 floor that made the knob meaningless is gone (its removal reverted in 11e5779b) and the silent-discard behaviour above is live again on a C++17 configure.
  - policy, not defect: what SHOULD happen when the knob cannot be honoured (keep the silent no-op, make it a hard error, or retire it) is a decision that only becomes available if quickcpplib ever drops C++14 outright. It is a policy question about a knob that is dead only on a C++17 build, not a defect to fix while C++14 is supported.
  - obsolete now: the option, the bundled byte-lite tree and its `ensure_git_subrepo()` caller were deleted (`52d33dcf`, "headers: delete the four C++17-provided polyfills and their knobs"), together with the akrzemi1/Optional and string_view trees. Removing them is legitimate because C++17 is now the default and C++14 is an explicit opt-in mode (`QUICKCPPLIB_MIN_CXX_STANDARD=14`, which Outcome sets); Outcome uses none of byte/optional/string_view/pmr. The knob no longer exists, so there is nothing left to discard silently. `QUICKCPPLIB_USE_SYSTEM_SPAN_LITE` is the only surviving USE_SYSTEM knob and its own rows stay open.

- **[P1] (obsolete) pmr::polymorphic_allocator C++14 emulation default-constructs with a null resource and segfaults on allocate()** — `include/quickcpplib/memory_resource.hpp:145`
  - also: `include/quickcpplib/memory_resource.hpp:170` (was P2/open) pmr emulation's polymorphic_allocator default-constructs with a null resource and segfaults instead of using a default resource like std::pmr
  - also: `include/quickcpplib/memory_resource.hpp:170` (was P1/open) polymorphic_allocator::allocate multiplies n*sizeof(T) without an overflow check, silently requesting a 0-byte block
  - triaged: confirmed a default-constructed polymorphic_allocator<T> has resource()==nullptr and allocate() segfaults (exit 139)
  - reverted: deleting this whole file (`headers: delete the memory_resource polyfill`) was itself REVERTED (the `Revert "headers: delete the memory_resource polyfill"` commit). Outcome must still build at C++14 and quickcpplib is shared between Outcome (C++14) and LLFIO (C++17), so the C++14 `memory_resource`/`monotonic_buffer_resource`/`polymorphic_allocator` emulation is back, `QUICKCPPLIB_NAMESPACE::pmr` exists again, and both defects above are live code once more: a default-constructed `polymorphic_allocator<T>` still has `resource() == nullptr` and still segfaults on `allocate()`, and `allocate()` still multiplies `n * sizeof(T)` without an overflow check. `#include <memory_resource>`/`std::pmr` is now one of two supported spellings, not the only one, and the configure-time C++17 floor that closed this class of defect is gone (reverted in 11e5779b).
  - policy note: whether to repair the emulation (give `polymorphic_allocator` a default resource, check the multiplication) or to retire it when C++14 support is eventually dropped is a decision for the user, not something this sweep may settle by deleting the file. Deleting it was tried and reverted because it broke Outcome's C++14 configure.
  - obsolete now: the user has settled the policy. `include/quickcpplib/memory_resource.hpp` was deleted outright (`52d33dcf`): no emulation and no alias remain. It had exactly one consumer in the tree, `test/bitwise_trie.cpp` (8 references); that test now includes `<memory_resource>` behind `#if __cplusplus >= 201703L` and is excluded from the opt-in C++14 mode with a visible configure-time STATUS message naming it. Outcome has zero pmr references. Removal is legitimate now because C++14 is an explicit opt-in compatibility mode, not the default, and the only consumer is C++17-only.
